profile.research_note: [batch narration moved out of reading 2026-09-02] This CyrusOne cluster sits in the Cincinnati metro area, spanning Cincinnati, Lebanon, and Butler and Warren Counties in Ohio and Florence, Kentucky just across the Ohio River. This is CyrusOne home market: Wikipedia coverage states Cincinnati Bell purchased CyrusOne for 525 million dollars in 2010 and later divested its remaining stake in 2015 after the company IPO in 2013. CyrusOne was originally founded in July 2000 by David Ferdman and Larry Bursten. The company was taken private again in 2022 when Kohlberg Kravis Roberts and Global Infrastructure Partners acquired it for 15 billion dollars. No building specific address or individual MW figures were located in available sourcing this session.
profile.campus_sqft_context: CyrusOne's centrally located CIN2 data center campus provides colocation, backup and recovery. Located near downtown Cincinnati, OH, CyrusOne's CIN2 data center is conveniently located 15 minutes from Greater Cincinnati and the Northern Kentucky International airports. As Cincinnati's primary carrier hotel facility, CIN2 offers 143,778 sq. ft. of IT technical space and is High-Performance Computing (HPC) capable. The center's design includes closed loop chilled water cooling with redundant feeds for makeup water, comprehensive security measures, and is on FEMA's priority list. The facility provides production colocation, backup and recovery, and business continuity solutions with proven reliability.

reading.body:
CyrusOne CIN2 publishes 11 MW of IT capacity in downtown Cincinnati, making it the second-largest disclosed data center in Ohio and roughly 28 percent of the state's published capacity.

The facility occupies 143,778 square feet of IT technical space and uses closed-loop chilled water cooling, a requirement for sustained high-density compute. At typical AI training density of 40 kW per rack, 11 MW supports approximately 275 racks. At standard colocation density of 10 kW per rack, it supports roughly 1,100 racks. The published megawatt figure is a hard ceiling on simultaneous load regardless of the facility's stated HPC capability.

Four certifications determine what workloads CIN2 can legally host: PCI DSS for payment-card processing, HIPAA for protected health information, ISO 27001 for certified information-security management, and FISMA for certain federal government work. This compliance posture qualifies the facility for regulated-industry AI inference and data pipelines. Which tenants actually occupy the space is not disclosed.

For Ohio-scale context, only five of 76 mapped data center facilities in the state publish a capacity figure. Those five sum to 38.6 MW. CIN2's share reflects the limits of disclosure as much as infrastructure reality, because most facilities publish no data. For regulated AI workloads requiring Midwest network proximity, 11 MW is sufficient for inference and moderate-scale analytics but constrains large-scale model training.
